definition: Refining crude oil into gasoline necessarily also produces every other refined product simultaneously, so a refiner cannot isolate output to just one product without risking oversupply of the co-products.
core_idea: Because distillation and cracking of a barrel of crude yields a whole slate of products at once, a refiner responding to high gasoline prices by increasing throughput also increases output of all other refined products, which can flood those other product markets.
key_points: It is impossible to produce a single refined product (e.g., gasoline only) without producing the others at the same time.
Increasing refinery output to capture higher gasoline prices raises supply of all other refined products too.
This can create a risk of glutting the market for the refinery's other (non-target) products.
relationships: Directly follows from the distillation/cracking process producing a full product slate from each barrel
trading_implications: Gasoline price rallies can indirectly pressure other refined product prices lower as refiners ramp output to capture gasoline margins, a cross-product effect worth tracking in refined products trading.
caveats: A refiner cannot simply 'dial in' higher gasoline output in isolation — the joint-product nature of distillation means all co-products scale together.
